tool_arguments.query: Microsoft FY2024 annual report capital expenditure AI data center spending

events.content: Microsoft FY2024 annual report capital expenditure AI data center spending

Microsoft’s FY2024 Q3 (quarter ended March 31, 2024) capital expenditure—including finance leases—was **$14.0 billion**, explicitly directed to cloud demand and scaling AI infrastructure; cash paid for property, plant and equipment was **$11.0 billion**. [[1]] 

This represented a **$2.5 billion, or 21.7%, sequential increase** from FY2024 Q2’s $11.5 billion capex including finance leases; cash PP&E spending increased $1.3 billion, or 13.4%, from $9.7 billion. [[2]] [[1]] 

Management characterized near-term AI demand as slightly above available capacity, said it was continuing to bring capacity online, and guided for capex to rise **materially sequentially in FY2024 Q4**, driven by cloud and AI infrastructure investment. [[1]] 

The spending was occurring alongside strong cloud demand: Azure and other cloud-services revenue grew **31% year over year**, with AI services contributing **7 percentage points** to that growth, while Intelligent Cloud revenue rose **21%** to **$26.7 billion**. [[1]] 

Microsoft also said FY2025 capex would exceed FY2024 capex, subject to demand and adoption signals, indicating that the Q3 buildout was part of a continuing data-center and AI-capacity expansion rather than a one-quarter surge. [[1]]

Sources:
[S1.1] Earnings FY 2024 q3 — https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/events/fy-2024/earnings-fy-2024-q3
[S1.2] Microsoft Fiscal Year 2024 Second Quarter Earnings Conference Call — https://microsoft.com/en-us/investor/events/fy-2024/earnings-fy-2024-q2.aspx

**Microsoft FY2026 Q1 AI/data-center spending** — for the quarter ended **September 30, 2025**, Microsoft reported **$34.9 billion of capital expenditures**, explicitly attributing the spend to demand for its cloud and AI offerings. [[1]]

- About **half of total capex**—approximately **$17.5 billion**—went to short-lived assets, principally GPUs and CPUs, supporting Azure demand, first-party applications and AI solutions, internal R&D, and replacement of end-of-life server/network equipment. [[1]]
- The other approximately **$17.5 billion** was long-lived infrastructure expected to support monetization for 15 years or more; this included **$11.1 billion of finance leases**, primarily for large data-center sites. [[1]]
- Cash payments for property, plant and equipment were **$19.4 billion**, versus $14.9 billion in FY2025 Q1; the difference between the $34.9 billion capex measure and cash PP&E payments chiefly reflected finance leases and the timing of equipment receipts versus payment. [[1]] [[2]]
- On Microsoft’s cash-flow statement, reported additions to property and equipment were **$19.394 billion**, a **30.0% year-over-year** increase from **$14.923 billion**. [[2]]
- On the broader management capex definition, the **$34.9 billion** was **74.5% higher year over year** than the **$20.0 billion** reported in FY2025 Q1, which also included finance leases. [[1]] [[3]]
- The Q1 figure equaled roughly **44.9% of quarterly revenue** of $77.673 billion, underscoring the unusually capital-intensive nature of Microsoft’s AI capacity buildout. [[4]] [[1]]
- Microsoft also disclosed **$106.2 billion of additional, not-yet-commenced leases**, primarily for data centers, as of September 30, 2025; those leases are scheduled to commence between FY2026 and FY2031. [[5]]
- Management said it planned to increase total AI capacity by **more than 80% in FY2026** and to **roughly double its total data-center footprint over the subsequent two years**. [[1]]
- For the following quarter, Microsoft guided that total capex would rise sequentially and that FY2026 capex growth would exceed FY2025’s growth rate, citing accelerating demand, a growing RPO balance, and increased GPU/CPU spending. [[1]]

tool_arguments.query: Alphabet FY2024 Q4 capital expenditure AI data center spending

events.content: Alphabet FY2024 Q4 capital expenditure AI data center spending

**Alphabet’s Q3 FY2025 AI-infrastructure spending accelerated sharply:** reported capital expenditure was **$24.0 billion** for the quarter ended September 30, 2025, versus **$13.0 billion** in Q3 2024—an increase of approximately **85% year over year**. [[1, 2]]

- The “vast majority” of Q3 capex went to **technical infrastructure**, with roughly **60% ($14.4 billion)** directed to **servers** and **40% ($9.6 billion)** to **data-center and networking equipment**. [[1]]
- Alphabet’s 10-Q defines technical infrastructure as servers and network equipment supporting computing, storage, networking—including AI—and data-center land and building construction; therefore, the $24 billion is best viewed as AI-enabled infrastructure spending rather than a company-disclosed, AI-only capex figure. [[3]]
- Google Cloud’s Q3 revenue rose **34% to $15.2 billion**, with growth driven in part by enterprise AI infrastructure and AI solutions, while Cloud backlog increased by **$49 billion sequentially**. [[1]]
- Management said supply would remain tight in Q4 2025 and 2026 despite faster server deployments and data-center construction, underpinning continued aggressive capacity investment. [[1]]

**FY2025 outlook:** Alphabet raised expected full-year capex to **$91–$93 billion**, from its prior **$85 billion** outlook. [[1]] Through the first nine months of 2025, purchases of property and equipment were **$63.596 billion**, compared with **$38.259 billion** in the comparable 2024 period. [[3]]

**Profit-and-cash-flow implications:** Q3 depreciation rose **$1.6 billion year over year to $5.6 billion**, or **41%**, and Alphabet expected depreciation growth to accelerate modestly in Q4 as the enlarged infrastructure base enters service. [[1]] Management also indicated that 2026 capex would increase significantly, with specifics to follow at its Q4 results. [[1]]

Sources:
[S7.1] Alphabet Investor Relations - 2025 Q3 Earnings Call — https://abc.xyz/investor/events/event-details/2025/2025-Q3-Earnings-Call-2025-4OI4Bac_Q9/default.aspx

events.content: Alphabet FY2024 full year capital expenditure AI data center

Alphabet spent **$35.7 billion of CapEx in Q1 FY2026** (quarter ended March 31, 2026), with the “overwhelming majority” directed to technical infrastructure supporting AI opportunities. [[1]] 

Within that technical-infrastructure spending, approximately **60% was servers**—including AI compute—and **40% was data centers and networking equipment**; Alphabet did not disclose the technical-infrastructure subtotal, so these percentages should not be applied mechanically to total CapEx. [[1]] 

For FY2026, Alphabet raised CapEx guidance to **$180 billion–$190 billion**, from **$175 billion–$185 billion**, incorporating investment associated with the Intersect acquisition that closed in March. [[1]] 

Management attributed the investment intensity to “unprecedented” internal and external demand for AI compute, while Google Cloud revenue rose **63% year over year** to more than **$20 billion** and backlog reached more than **$460 billion**. [[1]]

Sources:

tool_arguments.query: Amazon FY2024 Q4 capital expenditure AI data center spending

events.content: Amazon FY2024 Q4 capital expenditure AI data center spending

Amazon’s **Q3 FY2025 cash capital expenditure was $34.2 billion**, versus **$21.3 billion in Q3 FY2024**, a roughly **61% year-over-year increase**. [[1]] [[2]] 

For the first nine months of FY2025, cash CapEx reached **$89.9 billion**, and management raised its FY2025 expectation to approximately **$125 billion**, with spending expected to increase again in 2026. [[1]] 

Management said the spending **primarily relates to AWS**, including capacity for demand in **AI and core cloud services**, custom AI silicon such as **Trainium**, and technology infrastructure that also supports Amazon’s North America and International businesses. [[1]] 

The reported cash-flow-line item, “purchases of property and equipment,” was **$35.095 billion in Q3** and **$92.297 billion year-to-date**; the difference from the $34.2 billion “cash CapEx” figure reflects Amazon’s broader management definition and cash-flow timing/other capital items. [[2]] [[1]] 

The balance-sheet evidence points to a heavily AWS/data-center-oriented buildout: AWS property and equipment, net rose from **$110.7 billion at December 31, 2024** to **$165.1 billion at September 30, 2025**, while Amazon says technology-infrastructure assets are allocated by usage with the **majority allocated to AWS**. [[2]] 

Amazon did not disclose a precise stand-alone “AI data-center” dollar amount for Q3; therefore, the most defensible interpretation is that AI/data-center spending constituted the primary use of the $34.2 billion quarterly cash-CapEx program, rather than treating the entire amount as AI-only spending. [[1]]

Sources:
[S9.1] Amazon (AMZN) Q3 2025 Earnings Call Transcript — https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2025/10/31/amazon-amzn-q3-2025-earnings-call-transcript/

tool_arguments.query: Meta FY2024 full year capital expenditure AI data center

events.content: Meta FY2024 full year capital expenditure AI data center

**Meta Platforms — Q1 FY2026 AI/data-center spending**

- Meta spent **$19.84 billion** of capital expenditures in Q1 2026 (three months ended March 31), including principal payments on finance leases; management attributed this to investments in **servers, data centers, and network infrastructure**. [[1]] [[2]]

- Following the quarter, Meta raised its FY2026 capex outlook to **$125–145 billion**, from **$115–135 billion** previously—an increase of **$10 billion at both ends** of the range. [[1]] [[3]]

- The revised outlook is primarily due to expected **higher component prices**—with management specifically highlighting memory pricing—and, secondarily, incremental **data-center costs** to create capacity for future years. [[3]] [[4]]

- Q1 operating expenses were **$33.4 billion, up 35% year over year**; infrastructure-cost growth reflected higher depreciation, data-center operating costs, and third-party cloud spending. [[3]]

- Meta characterized compute as strategically central to more capable AI models and new products, and said it is expanding its owned data-center footprint, securing component supply, and adding cloud capacity scheduled to come online during 2026 and 2027. [[3]]

- Those multiyear cloud arrangements and infrastructure purchase agreements produced a **$107 billion quarter-over-quarter increase in contractual commitments**, which is a commitment measure rather than Q1 cash capex. [[3]]

**Analyst read-through:** Meta’s Q1 result confirms a substantial acceleration in AI-infrastructure investment, but the FY2026 capex-guide increase was predominantly an **input-cost / component-inflation revision**, rather than solely a new demand-driven buildout; incremental future-capacity data-center spending was explicitly a lesser contributor. [[3]] [[4]]

**Alphabet’s Q3 FY2025 AI-infrastructure spending accelerated sharply:** reported capital expenditure was **$24.0 billion** for the quarter ended September 30, 2025, versus **$13.0 billion** in Q3 2024—an increase of approximately **85% year over year**. [[1, 2]]

- The “vast majority” of Q3 capex went to **technical infrastructure**, with roughly **60% ($14.4 billion)** directed to **servers** and **40% ($9.6 billion)** to **data-center and networking equipment**. [[1]]
- Alphabet’s 10-Q defines technical infrastructure as servers and network equipment supporting computing, storage, networking—including AI—and data-center land and building construction; therefore, the $24 billion is best viewed as AI-enabled infrastructure spending rather than a company-disclosed, AI-only capex figure. [[3]]
- Google Cloud’s Q3 revenue rose **34% to $15.2 billion**, with growth driven in part by enterprise AI infrastructure and AI solutions, while Cloud backlog increased by **$49 billion sequentially**. [[1]]
- Management said supply would remain tight in Q4 2025 and 2026 despite faster server deployments and data-center construction, underpinning continued aggressive capacity investment. [[1]]

**FY2025 outlook:** Alphabet raised expected full-year capex to **$91–$93 billion**, from its prior **$85 billion** outlook. [[1]] Through the first nine months of 2025, purchases of property and equipment were **$63.596 billion**, compared with **$38.259 billion** in the comparable 2024 period. [[3]]

**Profit-and-cash-flow implications:** Q3 depreciation rose **$1.6 billion year over year to $5.6 billion**, or **41%**, and Alphabet expected depreciation growth to accelerate modestly in Q4 as the enlarged infrastructure base enters service. [[1]] Management also indicated that 2026 capex would increase significantly, with specifics to follow at its Q4 results. [[1]]

private_messages.content:
Amazon’s **Q3 FY2025 cash capital expenditure was $34.2 billion**, versus **$21.3 billion in Q3 FY2024**, a roughly **61% year-over-year increase**. [[1]] [[2]] 

For the first nine months of FY2025, cash CapEx reached **$89.9 billion**, and management raised its FY2025 expectation to approximately **$125 billion**, with spending expected to increase again in 2026. [[1]] 

Management said the spending **primarily relates to AWS**, including capacity for demand in **AI and core cloud services**, custom AI silicon such as **Trainium**, and technology infrastructure that also supports Amazon’s North America and International businesses. [[1]] 

The reported cash-flow-line item, “purchases of property and equipment,” was **$35.095 billion in Q3** and **$92.297 billion year-to-date**; the difference from the $34.2 billion “cash CapEx” figure reflects Amazon’s broader management definition and cash-flow timing/other capital items. [[2]] [[1]] 

The balance-sheet evidence points to a heavily AWS/data-center-oriented buildout: AWS property and equipment, net rose from **$110.7 billion at December 31, 2024** to **$165.1 billion at September 30, 2025**, while Amazon says technology-infrastructure assets are allocated by usage with the **majority allocated to AWS**. [[2]] 

Amazon did not disclose a precise stand-alone “AI data-center” dollar amount for Q3; therefore, the most defensible interpretation is that AI/data-center spending constituted the primary use of the $34.2 billion quarterly cash-CapEx program, rather than treating the entire amount as AI-only spending. [[1]]

private_messages.content:
**Meta Platforms — Q1 FY2026 AI/data-center spending**

- Meta spent **$19.84 billion** of capital expenditures in Q1 2026 (three months ended March 31), including principal payments on finance leases; management attributed this to investments in **servers, data centers, and network infrastructure**. [[1]] [[2]]

- Following the quarter, Meta raised its FY2026 capex outlook to **$125–145 billion**, from **$115–135 billion** previously—an increase of **$10 billion at both ends** of the range. [[1]] [[3]]

- The revised outlook is primarily due to expected **higher component prices**—with management specifically highlighting memory pricing—and, secondarily, incremental **data-center costs** to create capacity for future years. [[3]] [[4]]

- Q1 operating expenses were **$33.4 billion, up 35% year over year**; infrastructure-cost growth reflected higher depreciation, data-center operating costs, and third-party cloud spending. [[3]]

- Meta characterized compute as strategically central to more capable AI models and new products, and said it is expanding its owned data-center footprint, securing component supply, and adding cloud capacity scheduled to come online during 2026 and 2027. [[3]]

- Those multiyear cloud arrangements and infrastructure purchase agreements produced a **$107 billion quarter-over-quarter increase in contractual commitments**, which is a commitment measure rather than Q1 cash capex. [[3]]

**Analyst read-through:** Meta’s Q1 result confirms a substantial acceleration in AI-infrastructure investment, but the FY2026 capex-guide increase was predominantly an **input-cost / component-inflation revision**, rather than solely a new demand-driven buildout; incremental future-capacity data-center spending was explicitly a lesser contributor. [[3]] [[4]]
